description: Index suggestions recorded by SQL Server's optimizer, merged with each other and checked against existing indexes.
title: Missing indexes

description: Heavy queries whose plan reads a large table in full and keeps only the rows matching a filter that no index supports.
title: Scans an index would avoid

description: Indexes that are maintained on every write but no query has read since usage counters were reset.
title: Unused indexes

description: Indexes with the same keys as another index, or whose keys are a leading part of a wider one.
title: Duplicate and redundant indexes

description: Foreign key columns with no index starting with them, which makes deletes on the parent and joins from the child slow.
title: Foreign keys without an index

description: Two indexes that lead with the same column where one is barely read: queries that use it can almost always use the other.
title: Overlapping indexes

description: Tables with many secondary indexes that are written a lot: every insert updates each index.
title: Many indexes on write-heavy tables

description: Large tables that queries read in full many times a day, from the table scan counters.
title: Tables read in full over and over

description: Plan-forcing recommendations from automatic tuning, forced plans and Query Store hints that stopped applying, and automatic plan correction left off.
title: SQL Server's own tuning advice

description: The same statement sent many times with different literal values (or value-list lengths), so the database compiles and tracks each copy separately; and plan caches filled with single-use plans.
title: Statements with literals baked in

description: Single queries that take a large share of database time, with what their plan spends it on.
title: Queries that dominate database time

description: Tiny queries executed so often that the round trips cost more than the work, typically a loop in application code.
title: Chatty queries (N+1)

description: Implicit conversions, spills, missing join predicates and missing statistics in the plans of heavy queries.
title: Plan warnings

description: Key lookups, functions on filtered columns, leading wildcards, NOT IN, scalar functions, eager spools, misestimates and repeated loops in the plans of queries that matter.
title: Plan insights

description: Queries whose current plan is much slower than a plan they used before.
title: Plan regressions

description: Queries whose runs became much slower at some point in the window, with when it started and whether a plan change coincides. Needs Query Store history or a few earlier scans.
title: Queries that got slower

description: Queries whose duration swings wildly between runs with the same plan, a sign of parameter sensitivity or blocking.
title: Unstable queries

description: Statements whose run time depends heavily on the values they run with: two plans used side by side, one fast and one slow (SQL Server Query Store), or a long tail in the run-time histogram (MySQL). Single-plan variance on any engine is `unstable-query`.
title: Queries that are fast for most calls and slow for some

description: Statements whose sorts, hashes or temporary tables outgrow memory and spill to disk.
title: Queries writing temp files

description: Tables whose optimizer statistics are far behind their data, which leads to bad row estimates and plans.
title: Stale statistics

description: Heaps grow forwarded records and can't be read in key order; most OLTP tables should be clustered.
title: Large tables without a clustered index

description: Tables carrying many dead tuples, which bloat storage and slow scans.
title: Dead rows and lagging autovacuum

description: Transaction ID age approaching the point where Postgres stops accepting writes to protect data.
title: Transaction ID wraparound risk

description: Database and server settings that commonly hurt performance or hide the data needed to diagnose it.
title: Configuration

description: Deadlocks in the last day, grouped by pattern (key lookup, opposite order, read-then-update, lock escalation, parallelism) with the fix that removes them. SQL Server reads system_health, MySQL the latest InnoDB report, Postgres only keeps a counter.
title: Deadlocks

description: Statements whose memory grant (reserved before they run, for sorts and hashes) is many times what they use, so other queries queue for memory.
title: Queries that reserve far more memory than they use

description: Memory-grant waits (RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE) take a real share of waiting, or queries were queueing for a grant when the scan ran.
title: Queries waiting in line for memory

description: A large share of batches compile a new plan instead of reusing one, which costs CPU on every call.
title: Plans compiled over and over

description: SQL Server sessions waiting for a worker thread (THREADPOOL), or PostgreSQL/MySQL connections close to max_connections.
title: Running out of workers or connections

description: The oldest open transaction keeps old row versions alive: the SQL Server version store, PostgreSQL's VACUUM horizon, or InnoDB's undo history.
title: A long open transaction holds cleanup back

description: Queries that spend much of their time waiting for the application to take results (ASYNC_NETWORK_IO), usually because they return large result sets.
title: Results the application reads slowly

description: Azure SQL Database resources (CPU, data IO, log writes, workers) at the tier's limit for a real part of the last hour.
title: Hitting the cloud tier's limits

description: Many checkpoints start because WAL filled max_wal_size rather than on schedule, causing write spikes.
title: Checkpoints forced early

description: InnoDB row-lock waits are frequent and long, from long transactions or updates that scan instead of using an index.
title: Transactions waiting for row locks

description: Statements whose runs end in an error or are cancelled by the client (usually a command timeout): Query Store's aborted and exception runs, performance_schema's errors per digest. PostgreSQL keeps no per-statement error count.
title: Queries that fail or time out

description: Statements where planning (PostgreSQL, with pg_stat_statements.track_planning on) or compiling (SQL Server Query Store) takes a large part of their time, usually because the plan isn't reused.
title: Queries that spend their time being planned

description: Statements where PostgreSQL's JIT compilation (pg_stat_statements jit_* columns, 15+) takes a large part of their run time: usually short queries whose cost the planner overestimates.
title: JIT compilation that costs more than it saves

description: Statements that write a large share of the WAL (PostgreSQL 13+) or transaction log (SQL Server 2017+), or many kilobytes of it per row changed. Log volume drives replication lag, backup size and checkpoints. MySQL keeps no redo bytes per statement.
title: Writes that produce most of the log

description: Statements that spend a large part of their time waiting for locks other sessions hold: Query Store's lock waits per query, MySQL and MariaDB lock time per digest. PostgreSQL keeps no lock time per statement; Live shows blocking as it happens.
title: Queries that spend their time waiting for locks

description: Reads that send tens of thousands of rows to the application on every run, with an estimate in bytes from the plan's row width where the engine gives one.
title: Queries that return huge results

description: Indexes where sessions waited a long time for row and page locks, and where locks escalated to the whole table (sys.dm_db_index_operational_stats). MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL keep no lock waits per table; see lock-time and Live.
title: Rows that many sessions fight over

description: Indexes keyed on an ever-increasing value (identity, sequence, insert time) where concurrent inserts wait for the latch on the last page (PAGELATCH_EX).
title: Inserts that queue for the last page

description: SQL Server foreign keys and check constraints added or re-enabled WITH NOCHECK (or switched off), and PostgreSQL check constraints added NOT VALID. MySQL and MariaDB don't use constraints when planning.
title: Constraints the optimizer can't rely on

description: Columns that heavy queries filter on with no index leading on them and no histogram (MySQL 8 COLUMN_STATISTICS, MariaDB mysql.column_stats), so the optimizer assumes a fixed share of rows match.
title: Filter columns the optimizer has to guess about

description: Tables where few updates are HOT (heap-only): each other update writes a new entry in every index and leaves cleanup for VACUUM. Says whether pages are too full (fillfactor) or an indexed column changes (PostgreSQL 16+ tells them apart).
title: Updates that rewrite every index

description: Tables whose pages hold far fewer rows than they could, estimated from row counts and column widths in pg_stats (no extension needed). Every scan still reads the empty space.
title: Tables that are mostly empty space

description: Average read and write latency per database file since startup: sys.dm_io_virtual_file_stats, pg_stat_io (16+, with track_io_timing), performance_schema file I/O.
title: Storage that's slow to read or write

description: New connections per second since startup (SQL Server logins, PostgreSQL 14+ sessions, MySQL and MariaDB Connections), with how long sessions last and how many came from a pool where the engine says.
title: Applications that connect for every request

description: Replicas far behind the primary or stopped, and PostgreSQL replication slots that keep WAL for a consumer that's gone: pg_stat_replication, availability group replica states, SHOW REPLICA STATUS.
title: Replicas that fall behind

description: SQL Server 2019+ can keep each query's last actual plan (LAST_QUERY_PLAN_STATS) and report live per-operator progress (LIGHTWEIGHT_QUERY_PROFILING).
title: Actual plans without re-running queries
